scenarios.title: The login check that never matches
scenarios.situation: A username comparison with == works for literals in unit tests but fails for input read from the console.
scenarios.prompt: Why does == fail, and what is the correct comparison?
evidence:
String input = scanner.nextLine();
if (input == "admin") { grant(); }  // false for runtime strings
choices: == compares object references — use input.equals("admin"); literals may be interned, which is why tests accidentally passed
Strings from I/O are char[] — convert with new String(input) first
== works for strings but not for scanner input — call scanner.next() instead
String comparison requires compareTo — equals() only works for enums
scenarios.why: == on objects tests reference identity. String literals are interned (one shared instance per distinct literal), so == can appear to work in tests, but a runtime-built string is a different object with equal content. equals() compares content — always use it for value comparison. (For null-safety, "admin".equals(input) avoids NPE.)
scenarios.hint: What does == compare for objects — the characters, or which objects they are?

scenarios.title: The percentage that is always zero
scenarios.situation: A progress reporter computes done/total*100 as ints and always displays 0% until the very end.
scenarios.prompt: Why is the percentage zero, and how do you fix it?
evidence: int pct = done / total * 100;  // done < total -> 0 * 100 = 0
choices: done/total is integer division, truncating to 0 before the multiplication — cast first: (int)(done * 100.0 / total)
int arithmetic overflows at 100 — use long for pct
Multiplication must come first textually — write 100 * done / total as int math
The expression is evaluated right-to-left — add parentheses around done/total
scenarios.why: With int operands, done/total truncates toward zero — any proper fraction becomes 0, and 0*100 stays 0. Promoting one operand to double before dividing (done * 100.0 / total) performs floating-point division; cast back to int for display. (100 * done / total also works in int math but risks overflow for huge values.)
scenarios.hint: What is the value of done/total before the *100 ever runs?

scenarios.title: The switch that must produce a value
scenarios.situation: A refactored method needs a switch to yield a value. The old statement-switch with a mutable result variable is verbose and error-prone.
scenarios.prompt: How do switch expressions (Java 14+) improve this?
choices: Arrow-case switch expressions yield a value, forbid fallthrough, and the compiler checks exhaustiveness
Switch expressions are slower — keep the statement form for hot paths
Arrow syntax only works for enums — int switches must use colons
Switch expressions cannot have a default — every case must be listed
scenarios.why: A switch expression is an expression: it produces a value, so no mutable accumulator is needed. Arrow cases (->) do not fall through, comma-separated labels group cases, and the compiler enforces exhaustiveness (all cases covered or a default present). yield is available for colon-style blocks that compute the value.
scenarios.hint: What three things does the arrow form give you that the colon form does not?

scenarios.title: The var that will not compile
scenarios.situation: A developer sprinkles var everywhere — on fields, method parameters, and a null initializer — and gets three different compile errors.
scenarios.prompt: Where is var actually allowed?
choices: var is only for local variables with an initializer the compiler can infer a type from — not fields, parameters, or null initializers
var works anywhere a type appears — the errors are a compiler bug
var requires the initializer to be a literal — method calls are not allowed
var infers Object for null — the code compiles with a warning
scenarios.why: var is not dynamic typing — it is compile-time type inference for local variables, and the compiler needs an initializer with a concrete type. Fields and parameters are part of a class's API contract, so they require explicit types. (var x = null gives the compiler nothing to infer.)
scenarios.hint: What information does the compiler need to fill in for var — and where is that information missing?

scenarios.title: The DTO with 60 lines of boilerplate
scenarios.situation: A data-carrier class has final fields, a constructor, getters, equals, hashCode, and toString — all hand-written, with a copy-paste bug in equals.
scenarios.prompt: Which Java 16+ feature generates all of this correctly?
evidence: record Point(int x, int y) {}  // canonical constructor, accessors, equals/hashCode/toString generated
choices: A record — the compiler generates the canonical constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString from the header
An interface with default methods — it generates the boilerplate at runtime
A sealed class — sealing triggers boilerplate generation
Records are syntax sugar for HashMap — put the fields in a map instead
scenarios.why: record Point(int x, int y) declares an immutable data carrier: the compiler synthesizes the constructor, x()/y() accessors, and value-based equals/hashCode/toString. Records are final (cannot be extended) and their components are final — custom validation goes in the compact constructor. Use them for DTOs, tuples, and value objects.
scenarios.hint: Which declaration turns a field list directly into a complete immutable value class?

scenarios.title: The cast after instanceof
scenarios.situation: Legacy code checks instanceof then casts on the next line — verbose, and a rename once left the cast pointing at the wrong type.
scenarios.prompt: How does pattern matching for instanceof (Java 16+) remove the cast?
choices: Pattern matching binds the cast variable in the same expression — no explicit cast, and the variable is in scope where the test passed
instanceof now returns the cast object instead of boolean — assign it directly
The pattern form is slower — keep the explicit cast in hot code
Pattern variables are always nullable — add a null check after binding
scenarios.why: shape instanceof Circle c tests and casts in one step, introducing c as a Circle wherever the pattern matched (flow scoping). It eliminates the duplicated type name where cast bugs hide, and the compiler rejects impossible patterns. (instanceof is false for null, so no NPE on the test.)
scenarios.hint: What two things did the old code do on two lines that the pattern does on one?

scenarios.title: The overload that pretended to override
scenarios.situation: A subclass meant to override notify(String) but declared notify(Object). The base version kept running with no compiler complaint.
scenarios.prompt: Which annotation turns this silent bug into a compile error?
choices: @Override — the compiler verifies an actual overridden method exists and fails the build otherwise
@Deprecated — marks the method as legacy so callers avoid it
@SuppressWarnings — hides the accidental overload warning
No annotation can help — rename the method to avoid confusion
scenarios.why: Without @Override, notify(Object) is just an overload — legal Java that silently does not participate in polymorphism. @Override asks the compiler to prove a matching supertype method exists; a signature mismatch becomes an error at the declaration. Apply it to every intended override, including interface implementations.
scenarios.hint: Which annotation makes the compiler check your intent to override, rather than trusting you?

scenarios.title: The interface that grew a method
scenarios.situation: A library interface needs a new method, but adding an abstract method would break every existing implementation.
scenarios.prompt: How do default methods evolve interfaces safely?
choices: default methods carry an implementation in the interface — existing implementers inherit it and keep compiling
Default methods are static — call them as Repository.saveAll(...)
Interfaces cannot have method bodies — use an abstract class instead
Mark the new method abstract and ship a migration guide
scenarios.why: A default method provides an implementation inside the interface, so adding one does not break existing implementers — they inherit it. Implementers may still override it. (Diamond conflicts — two interfaces providing the same default — must be resolved explicitly by the implementing class, which is the one sharp edge.)
scenarios.hint: What kind of interface method can add behavior without forcing every implementer to change?

scenarios.title: The immutable class that was not
scenarios.situation: An 'immutable' config class stores a Date passed by the caller. Callers mutate the Date afterward and the config silently changes.
scenarios.prompt: How do you make the class genuinely immutable?
choices: Defensively copy on the way in (and on the way out of getters) — new Date(d.getTime()); better, use immutable java.time types
final already guarantees immutability — the callers are misusing the API
Make the field static so all instances share one canonical Date
Clone is broken in Java — immutability of Dates is impossible
scenarios.why: final protects the reference, not the object: a final Date field still aliases a mutable Date the caller can change. True immutability requires copying mutable inputs at construction and returning copies (or immutable views) from getters. The modern fix is avoiding legacy mutable types entirely — java.time.Instant is immutable by design.
scenarios.hint: What does final lock down — the reference, or the object it points to?

scenarios.title: The key that cannot be found
scenarios.situation: A class overrides equals but not hashCode. Equal instances stored as HashMap keys cannot be retrieved.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the map lose entries with equal keys?
choices: HashMap buckets by hashCode first — equal objects with different identity hash codes land in different buckets, so equals is never consulted; always override hashCode with equals
HashMap uses == for keys — equals is irrelevant to maps
The map needs a custom Comparator — equals/hashCode are for sets only
String ids are interned — the bug is the new Key allocation
scenarios.why: Hash-based collections hash first and compare with equals only within a bucket. The contract is: equal objects must have equal hash codes. Overriding equals without hashCode leaves the default identity hash, so logically-equal keys scatter across buckets and lookups miss. IDEs generate both together for exactly this reason.
scenarios.hint: What does a HashMap check before it ever calls equals?

scenarios.title: The hierarchy that must stay closed
scenarios.situation: A payment-type hierarchy must allow exactly Card, Bank, and Crypto — no surprise subclasses from other teams that break an exhaustive switch.
scenarios.prompt: How do sealed classes (Java 17+) enforce a closed hierarchy?
evidence:
public sealed interface Payment permits Card, Bank, Crypto { }
// any other implementer: compile error
choices: sealed with permits lists every allowed subtype — the compiler rejects all others, and switches over the hierarchy can be exhaustive
Sealed classes cannot be implemented at all — use an enum instead
permits is documentation only — reflection can still add subtypes
Final classes already prevent extension — sealed adds nothing
scenarios.why: sealed declares a closed set of permitted direct subtypes; anything else is a compile error. Each permitted subtype must itself be final, sealed, or non-sealed (explicit choice). Combined with pattern-matching switch, the compiler can verify exhaustiveness — adding a new payment type breaks the switch loudly instead of silently.
scenarios.hint: Which modifier lets a type name exactly who may extend or implement it?

scenarios.title: The wrong abstraction
scenarios.situation: A team models 'can fly' as an abstract class, then discovers Penguins need swimming too — and Java has no multiple inheritance of classes.
scenarios.prompt: When do you choose an interface over an abstract class?
evidence:
abstract class Bird { abstract void fly(); }  // Penguin cannot extend Bird AND Swimmer
// interface Flyable { void fly(); } -- a class can implement many
choices: Interfaces model capabilities (can-do) and support multiple inheritance of type — abstract classes model is-a hierarchies with shared state
Abstract classes are faster — always prefer them for performance
Interfaces cannot have fields — use abstract classes whenever data is involved
There is no difference since Java 8 default methods — pick randomly
scenarios.why: A class extends exactly one class but implements many interfaces, so capabilities (Flyable, Swimmable) belong in interfaces while a true is-a backbone with shared state and constructor logic belongs in an abstract class. Default methods narrowed the gap, but state, constructors, and single-inheritance still distinguish them.
scenarios.hint: How many of each can one class have — and what does that imply for modeling capabilities versus identity?

scenarios.title: The generic array that will not compile
scenarios.situation: A generic cache tries to allocate new T[capacity] and the compiler refuses.
scenarios.prompt: Why can you not create arrays of a type parameter?
evidence:
class Cache<T> {
    T[] items = new T[16];  // error: generic array creation
choices: Type erasure: T does not exist at runtime, and arrays need a reifiable component type — use ArrayList<T> or Object[] with casts
Arrays of generics are allowed since Java 10 — upgrade the JDK
T[] requires T to be final — bound it as <T extends Final>
The syntax is new T[](16) — the brackets are misplaced
scenarios.why: Generics are erased at compile time: at runtime a Cache<String> is just Cache, so the JVM could not enforce new T[]'s type safety (arrays are covariant and reified, generics are invariant and erased — the combination is unsound). ArrayList<T> is the idiomatic replacement; internally it uses Object[] with checked casts.
scenarios.hint: What does T become after compilation — and what does an array need to know at runtime?

scenarios.title: The producer list you cannot add to
scenarios.situation: A method accepts List<? extends Number> to read numbers, but a teammate tries to add an Integer and the compiler rejects it.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the wildcard bound forbid adding?
choices: PECS: ? extends Number is a producer — the list could be List<Double>, so adding an Integer would corrupt it; use ? super Integer for consumers
Wildcard lists are immutable — wrap with Collections.unmodifiableList first
The compiler cannot verify autoboxing through wildcards — add ((Number)(Integer)1)
? extends Number means List<Number> exactly — the caller's List<Integer> should not compile
scenarios.why: ? extends Number means 'a List of some specific subtype of Number, we know not which' — it could be List<Double>, where an Integer does not belong. The compiler therefore forbids adds (except null). PECS: producer-extends (read from it), consumer-super (write to it — List<? super Integer> accepts Integer adds).
scenarios.hint: If the actual list is a List<Double>, what goes wrong when someone adds an Integer through your reference?

scenarios.title: The cache with a race-shaped hole
scenarios.situation: A hand-rolled cache does get-then-put with a null check. Under load, the expensive loader runs multiple times for the same key.
scenarios.prompt: Which Map method makes the check-and-load atomic?
evidence:
Value v = cache.get(key);
if (v == null) { v = load(key); cache.put(key, v); }  // racy on ConcurrentHashMap too
choices: computeIfAbsent(key, k -> load(k)) — the mapping function runs at most once per key atomically
putIfAbsent after a separate load — two calls are still atomic together
Synchronize the whole method — the only correct fix
getOrDefault with a precomputed default — defaults are lazy in Java
scenarios.why: computeIfAbsent performs the check-and-compute as one atomic operation (on ConcurrentHashMap, properly synchronized): if the key is absent, the mapping function runs and its result is installed — no window for a second thread to duplicate the load. The get/put pair has a check-then-act race even on concurrent maps.
scenarios.hint: What happens between your get and your put when two threads arrive at once?

scenarios.title: The immutable list someone mutated
scenarios.situation: A method returns List.of(...) and a caller adds to it, getting UnsupportedOperationException at runtime.
scenarios.prompt: What is the contract of List.of, and how do you get a modifiable copy?
choices: List.of returns an unmodifiable list — wrap it: new ArrayList<>(List.of(...)) for a mutable copy
List.of returns null for empty input — check for null before adding
The exception means the list is full — use List.of with a larger capacity
Unmodifiable is a compile-time property — the code should not compile
scenarios.why: The List.of/Set.of/Map.of factories (Java 9+) return structurally immutable collections — any mutator throws UnsupportedOperationException. They also reject null elements outright. When callers need to mutate, copy into an ArrayList (or collect with Collectors.toList(), whose mutability is the implementation's documented choice).
scenarios.hint: Is the immutability of List.of enforced by the type system, or at runtime — and what does that imply for the caller?

scenarios.title: The loop that removes and explodes
scenarios.situation: A cleanup loop removes expired sessions from a list with list.remove() inside a for-each, throwing ConcurrentModificationException.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the for-each fail, and what are the two correct patterns?
choices: Structural modification during iteration invalidates the iterator — use iterator.remove() explicitly, or removeIf(s -> s.expired())
For-each loops are read-only — convert to an indexed for loop and remove by index
The exception is thrown only for ArrayList — switch to LinkedList
Catch the exception and retry the loop until it completes
scenarios.why: Collection iterators are fail-fast: any structural change not made through the iterator itself trips ConcurrentModificationException on the next iterator operation. iterator.remove() is the sanctioned in-loop removal; Collection.removeIf (Java 8+) expresses the whole pass declaratively and handles the iterator protocol internally.
scenarios.hint: Who is allowed to structurally modify a collection mid-iteration — the loop body directly, or someone else?

scenarios.title: The sort that contradicts equals
scenarios.situation: A TreeSet of employees sorted by name silently drops two different employees who share a name.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the set treat them as duplicates?
choices: TreeSet uses the comparator (not equals) to decide duplication — comparing only by name makes same-named employees 'equal'; chain a tiebreaker (thenComparing(Employee::id))
TreeSet requires equals/hashCode — the comparator is ignored for duplicates
comparing() is unstable — use a hand-written Comparator class
Sets cannot hold duplicates by definition — use a List instead
scenarios.why: Sorted collections define equality via the comparator: compare(a,b)==0 means 'duplicate', regardless of equals(). With a name-only comparator, two Amys compare as 0 and the second add is dropped. The fix is a comparator consistent with equals — thenComparing(Employee::id) breaks the tie. The general rule: comparators used in sorted sets/maps should be consistent with equals.
scenarios.hint: How does a TreeSet decide two elements are the same — equals(), or something else?

scenarios.title: The pipeline that never runs
scenarios.situation: A stream pipeline with filter and map produces no output and the mapped function's side effects never happen.
scenarios.prompt: Why does nothing execute?
evidence:
orders.stream()
    .filter(o -> o.total() > 100)
    .map(o -> { audit(o); return o; });  // no terminal op: nothing runs
choices: Intermediate operations are lazy — without a terminal operation (forEach, collect, count) the pipeline never executes
Streams are single-threaded — the pipeline needs .parallel() to run
map with a block lambda is illegal — use a method reference
filter short-circuits the stream — remove the filter to see output
scenarios.why: filter/map/peek are intermediate: they only describe the pipeline. Execution is triggered by a terminal operation like forEach, collect, reduce, or count. This laziness enables fusion and short-circuiting (findFirst stops early), but a pipeline with no terminal op is dead code. (Also: side effects belong in forEach/peek for debugging, not in map.)
scenarios.hint: Which operations in the pipeline actually demand a result — and what happens if none is present?

scenarios.title: The variable the lambda cannot see
scenarios.situation: A lambda inside a loop tries to use the loop counter after it is reassigned, and the compiler rejects it.
scenarios.prompt: What restriction applies to captured local variables?
choices: Captured locals must be final or effectively final — use an AtomicInteger, a single-element array, or restructure with reduce()
Lambdas cannot access locals at all — make total a field
forEach lambdas run on other threads — locals are thread-confined
The restriction was removed in Java 17 — upgrade the JDK
scenarios.why: Lambdas capture local variables by value (a copy), so allowing later mutation would create two divergent truths. Java enforces this by requiring captured locals to be final or effectively final (never reassigned). For genuine accumulation, reduce() expresses the fold functionally, or an AtomicInteger provides a mutable holder.
scenarios.hint: Does the lambda see the variable, or a copy of its value — and what would reassignment mean for the copy?

scenarios.title: The Optional that threw anyway
scenarios.situation: Code wraps a lookup in Optional but calls get() unconditionally, throwing NoSuchElementException on misses — the same crash Optional was meant to prevent.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct way to consume an Optional?
evidence:
Optional<User> u = repo.find(id);
return u.get().name();  // throws when empty
choices: Never call get() blindly — use orElseThrow/map/orElse: return u.map(User::name).orElse("unknown")
Optional.get() is deprecated — the code should not compile
Wrap get() in try/catch NoSuchElementException — that is the intended pattern
Optional is only for streams — use null checks for repository lookups
scenarios.why: Optional is a container signaling 'value or absence' — calling get() without checking reintroduces the exact null-dereference-style crash it replaces. The API's combinators (map, flatMap, filter, orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow) handle both cases declaratively. (Also note orElse evaluates its argument eagerly — orElseGet takes a Supplier for lazy defaults.)
scenarios.hint: If you call get() without checking, what have you gained over a raw null check?

scenarios.title: The duplicate key that crashed collect
scenarios.situation: Collectors.toMap crashes with IllegalStateException: Duplicate key when two orders share a customer ID.
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle key collisions in toMap?
choices: Supply a merge function: toMap(Order::customerId, o -> o, (a, b) -> a) — or use groupingBy for one-to-many
toMap requires unique keys by contract — deduplicate the stream first with distinct()
Wrap the collect in try/catch and retry with a HashMap
Duplicate keys are impossible — the data must be corrupt
scenarios.why: The two-arg toMap throws on duplicate keys by design — silent overwriting would hide data loss. The three-arg overload takes a BinaryOperator merge function deciding which value wins (keep-first (a,b)->a, keep-last (a,b)->b, or combine). When one key maps to many values, Collectors.groupingBy(keyMapper) builds the Map<K, List<V>> directly.
scenarios.hint: Should a collector silently discard data on collision — and if not, who should decide the winner?

scenarios.title: The parallel stream that lost data
scenarios.situation: A parallel stream appends results to a shared ArrayList. Items go missing and the list sometimes corrupts.
scenarios.prompt: Why is the shared list unsafe, and what is the correct pattern?
evidence:
List<Result> out = new ArrayList<>();
items.parallelStream().map(this::compute).forEach(out::add);  // racy, unordered
choices: forEach with a shared mutable ArrayList is a data race — use collect(Collectors.toList()), which partitions and merges safely
parallelStream is broken for map — use sequential streams only
ArrayList.add is atomic — the missing items are a visibility issue; add volatile
forEachOrdered fixes thread safety — just switch the terminal op
scenarios.why: parallelStream splits work across threads; mutating a shared non-thread-safe ArrayList from forEach is a data race (lost updates, corruption). collect() is designed for this: each thread accumulates into its own container, then results merge. (forEachOrdered only fixes encounter order, not safety — and collect preserves order for ordered streams anyway.)
scenarios.hint: How many threads call out::add concurrently — and what does ArrayList promise about concurrent mutation?

scenarios.title: The lambda that is just a method call
scenarios.situation: A codebase is full of x -> helper.process(x) lambdas that add noise without adding logic.
scenarios.prompt: When can a lambda become a method reference, and what are the four forms?
evidence:
names.stream().map(s -> s.toUpperCase())  // -> names.stream().map(String::toUpperCase)
list.forEach(x -> System.out.println(x))  // -> list.forEach(System.out::println)
choices: When the lambda only forwards to one method — the four forms are Class::staticMethod, obj::instanceMethod, Class::instanceMethod, Class::new
Method references are always faster — replace every lambda with one
Only static methods can be referenced — instance methods need lambdas
Method references cannot take arguments — they work only for suppliers
scenarios.why: A lambda that does nothing but call a method (s -> s.toUpperCase()) is exactly a method reference (String::toUpperCase). The four forms: static (Integer::parseInt), bound instance (System.out::println), unbound instance (String::length — the stream element becomes the receiver), and constructor (ArrayList::new). They are equivalent in behavior to the lambda — the win is readability, not performance.
scenarios.hint: If the lambda body is a single method call forwarding its parameters, what shorter syntax says the same thing?

scenarios.title: The counter that loses counts
scenarios.situation: A hit counter incremented by many threads reports fewer hits than the access log shows.
scenarios.prompt: Why do increments go missing, and what is the minimal fix?
choices: hits++ is three operations (read, add, write) — interleavings lose updates; use AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()
int increments are atomic on 64-bit — the log must be double-counting
Static fields are thread-local — each thread has its own hits
The JIT reorders the increment — disable optimization with -Xint
scenarios.why: hits++ compiles to load, increment, store — between any two steps another thread can interleave and its update gets overwritten (lost update). AtomicInteger uses CAS (compare-and-set) hardware instructions to make the whole read-modify-write indivisible. (synchronized would also work but is heavier for a simple counter.)
scenarios.hint: How many machine steps does hits++ take — and what can another thread do between them?

scenarios.title: The deadlock that strikes on Fridays
scenarios.situation: Two services lock account A then B, and B then A. Under load the system freezes with both threads waiting forever.
scenarios.prompt: What causes the deadlock, and what ordering rule prevents it?
evidence:
// thread 1: synchronized(a) { synchronized(b) { transfer(a, b); } }
// thread 2: synchronized(b) { synchronized(a) { transfer(b, a); } }  // deadlock
choices: Circular wait — one of the Coffman conditions; enforce a global lock ordering (always lock the lower-id account first) to break the cycle
Synchronized blocks cannot nest — flatten them into one block
Deadlocks require three threads — two threads cannot deadlock
The fix is Thread.sleep between the locks to let the other thread finish
scenarios.why: Deadlock needs four conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait). Acquiring locks in opposite orders creates the circular wait. A global ordering — e.g., always lock the account with the smaller id first — makes cycles impossible. Alternatives: tryLock with timeout and backoff, or a single coarse lock when contention is low.
scenarios.hint: Draw the 'waits-for' graph of the two threads. What shape is it, and which acquisition rule prevents that shape?

scenarios.title: The pool sized for blocking calls
scenarios.situation: A service makes blocking HTTP calls on a 200-thread platform pool. Under spike load, requests queue and latency explodes.
scenarios.prompt: How do virtual threads (Java 21) change the sizing math?
choices: Virtual threads are cheap (KBs) and mount on carrier threads — blocking calls park the virtual thread without wasting a carrier, so thread-per-task replaces tuned pools
Virtual threads are faster CPUs — the same 200 threads do more work
Virtual threads eliminate the need for executors — call handle(req) directly
Blocking calls are forbidden on virtual threads — rewrite everything async
scenarios.why: Platform threads are expensive (~MB stacks, OS threads), so blocking I/O on them wastes a scarce resource — hence pool sizing. Virtual threads are JVM-managed and cheap; when one blocks, its carrier thread is freed for another virtual thread. Thread-per-task becomes viable again: no pool sizing, no queue tuning. (Do not pool virtual threads, and avoid pinning carriers with synchronized blocks around long I/O — use ReentrantLock instead.)
scenarios.hint: What is the scarce resource wasted when a platform thread blocks — and does a virtual thread waste it?

scenarios.title: The JVM that would not exit
scenarios.situation: A batch job's main method finishes, but the process hangs forever instead of exiting.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the executor keep the JVM alive, and what is the correct shutdown?
choices: Pool threads are non-daemon — call exec.shutdown() and awaitTermination, or use try-with-resources (ExecutorService is AutoCloseable since Java 19)
Executors must be static — local executors cannot be shut down
Call System.exit(0) at the end of main — the standard fix
Fixed pools cannot be shut down — use a cached pool instead
scenarios.why: The JVM exits only when all non-daemon threads finish; executor pool threads are non-daemon and idle-wait forever. shutdown() stops accepting tasks and lets submitted ones finish; awaitTermination bounds the wait. Since Java 19, ExecutorService extends AutoCloseable, so try (var exec = ...) { } shuts down automatically — the modern idiom.
scenarios.hint: What keeps a JVM alive after main returns — and whose threads are those?

scenarios.title: The flag the thread never saw
scenarios.situation: A worker loop checks a boolean stop flag set by another thread, but the worker never stops — it seems to read a stale cached value forever.
scenarios.prompt: Why is the update invisible, and what does volatile guarantee?
evidence:
boolean running = true;  // written by main thread, read by worker
while (running) { work(); }  // may never observe the write
choices: Without synchronization the write may sit in a CPU cache or be hoisted by the JIT — volatile establishes happens-before visibility for the flag
Booleans are not thread-safe in Java — use AtomicBoolean for any shared flag
The JIT caches running in a register — volatile prevents all JIT optimization
Visibility is guaranteed for all fields — the bug must be in work()
scenarios.why: The Java Memory Model allows threads to cache field values; without a happens-before edge, a write in one thread may never become visible to another (the JIT may even hoist the read out of the loop). volatile gives each read/write volatile semantics with happens-before ordering — the standard tool for a simple stop flag. (For read-modify-write like counters, volatile is not enough — that needs atomicity, i.e., AtomicInteger.)
scenarios.hint: What ordering guarantee connects a write in one thread to a read in another — and which keyword creates it for a simple flag?

scenarios.title: The ThreadLocal that ate the heap
scenarios.situation: After migrating to virtual threads, a ThreadLocal cache that was fine with 200 platform threads now holds a million entries and memory balloons.
scenarios.prompt: Why does ThreadLocal scale badly with virtual threads?
evidence:
static final ThreadLocal<Buffer> BUF = ThreadLocal.withInitial(Buffer::new);
// 200 platform threads: 200 buffers. 1M virtual threads: up to 1M buffers.
choices: ThreadLocal multiplies by thread count — with a virtual thread per task, per-thread state becomes per-task state; use explicit context parameters or scoped values instead
ThreadLocals leak on virtual threads — call remove() in a finally block and keep the pattern
Virtual threads share one ThreadLocal map — the entries collide and duplicate
ThreadLocal is deprecated for virtual threads — the code will not compile
scenarios.why: ThreadLocal was designed for expensive, long-lived platform threads where per-thread state is bounded. Virtual threads are cheap and numerous — a thread-per-task server can have millions over its life, turning each ThreadLocal into an unbounded per-task cache. Prefer passing context explicitly, or ScopedValue (Java 21+) for immutable request-scoped data with structured lifetime.
scenarios.hint: What did ThreadLocal cost multiply by when the thread count went from hundreds to millions?

scenarios.title: The package the module would not share
scenarios.situation: A modularized app fails at startup: 'package com.acme.internal is not visible' when another module touches an internal package.
scenarios.prompt: How do modules control package visibility?
choices: Modules encapsulate by default — only exported packages are visible to other modules; internal packages stay hidden even though they are public classes
All public classes are visible across modules — the error means the JAR is corrupt
exports is documentation — use requires transitive to fix visibility
Internal packages must be deleted — modules forbid non-exported code
scenarios.why: The module system (JPMS) enforces strong encapsulation: a public class in a non-exported package is inaccessible outside its module, even via reflection (without opens). exports declares the module's public API surface; everything else is implementation detail. This is the fix for JAR hell's 'everything public is public everywhere'.
scenarios.hint: What does a module hide by default — and what declaration opts a package out of hiding?

scenarios.title: The JAR that will not launch
scenarios.situation: java -jar app.jar fails with 'no main manifest attribute' though the Main class exists and compiles.
scenarios.prompt: What does the executable JAR need?
evidence:
$ java -jar app.jar
no main manifest attribute, in app.jar
choices: The manifest needs Main-Class: com.acme.Main (plus Class-Path for dependencies) — build tools generate it, or jar cfe app.jar com.acme.Main *.class
JARs cannot be executed — extract and run java -cp with the class files
The Main class must be in the default package — move it out of com.acme
java -jar requires a signed JAR — sign it with jarsigner first
scenarios.why: java -jar locates the entry point through the JAR manifest's Main-Class attribute (META-INF/MANIFEST.MF). Without it the JVM does not know which class to run. jar cfe sets it at packaging time; Maven/Gradle plugins (shade/spring-boot) generate full manifests including Class-Path. (Fat/uber JARs additionally unpack dependencies into the single archive.)
scenarios.hint: How does java -jar know which of your fifty classes contains main()?

scenarios.title: The stream left open on exception
scenarios.situation: File handles leak when a read throws midway — the close() at the method's end is skipped.
scenarios.prompt: Which construct guarantees resource closure?
choices: try-with-resources — any AutoCloseable declared in the try header is closed automatically, with suppressed-exception handling
A finally block calling close() — the only reliable pattern
Closeable resources are closed by the garbage collector — no code needed
Declare the reader outside try and close it after the catch blocks
scenarios.why: try-with-resources closes each resource in reverse declaration order when the block exits — normally, via return, or by exception. If both the body and close() throw, the close exception is suppressed (retrievable via getSuppressed()) rather than masking the original. Any class implementing AutoCloseable participates, including custom resources.
scenarios.hint: Which try header form ties a resource's lifetime to the block — and what happens to an exception thrown during close?

scenarios.title: The deserialization that broke after a deploy
scenarios.situation: A serialized object written by v1 cannot be read by v2 after a field was added — InvalidClassException: local class incompatible.
scenarios.prompt: What controls serialization compatibility, and what is the real fix?
choices: serialVersionUID versions the class's serialized form — declare it explicitly and evolve classes compatibly (added fields are tolerated); better, prefer a schema-based format (JSON) for long-lived data
Serialization is version-agnostic — the exception means the file is corrupt
Delete serialVersionUID — the JVM then accepts any version
Serializable classes cannot gain fields — keep the class frozen forever
scenarios.why: Without an explicit serialVersionUID, the JVM computes one from the class structure — any field change alters it and breaks deserialization. Declaring it explicitly opts into compatible evolution (added fields default, removed fields ignored). For durable storage or wire protocols, Java serialization is fragile and insecure-by-default; JSON/Avro/ProtoBuf with explicit schemas are the robust choice.
scenarios.hint: What identifies 'the same class' across versions during deserialization — and who should control that identifier?

scenarios.title: The config file found in the IDE but not in the JAR
scenarios.situation: new File("config/app.properties") works when run from the IDE but fails from the packaged JAR.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the file path break, and how do you load packaged resources?
choices: File paths are filesystem-relative; inside a JAR the resource is not a file — load it from the classpath with getResourceAsStream
JARs cannot contain properties files — move config outside the archive
The working directory differs — set -Duser.dir to the config folder
getResourceAsStream only works for images — properties need the File API
scenarios.why: new File(...) addresses the OS filesystem relative to the working directory — inside a JAR there is no config/app.properties file on disk. Classpath resources (getResource/getResourceAsStream) are resolved by the class loader, which reads them from directories or JAR entries transparently. Leading '/' means absolute within the classpath; without it, relative to the class's package.
scenarios.hint: Is the properties file a filesystem file when the app ships as a JAR — and what API reads 'from the classpath' regardless of packaging?

scenarios.title: The HTTP call with 40 lines of boilerplate
scenarios.situation: Legacy code uses HttpURLConnection with manual stream handling, timeouts set in two places, and no clean async option.
scenarios.prompt: What does java.net.http (Java 11+) provide?
choices: A fluent modern client: builders for client/request, BodyHandlers for response conversion, and sendAsync returning CompletableFuture
HttpClient is synchronous-only — async still needs raw threads
The new API only supports HTTP/1.1 — keep HttpURLConnection for HTTP/2
BodyHandlers.ofString loads the whole body — streaming is impossible
scenarios.why: java.net.http.HttpClient replaces the 1990s HttpURLConnection: immutable builders, first-class timeouts, HTTP/2 support by default, and BodyHandlers (ofString, ofInputStream, ofFile, discarding) separating transport from body conversion. sendAsync returns CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<T>> for non-blocking pipelines that compose with the rest of the async API.
scenarios.hint: Which API gives you builders, body handlers, and a CompletableFuture-based async send in one package?
